strengths: Addresses a clear and underexplored gap: existing 2D/video diffusion approaches to 3D scene generation struggle with multi-room, environment-scale consistency, especially in close-up and cross-room views. The proposed geometry-first decoupling (explicit mesh scaffold for structure + mesh-conditioned diffusion for appearance) is a sensible and well-motivated solution.

System design is comprehensive and each component is well justified: LLM-based floor-plan generation with spatial validity constraints, camera viewpoint scheduling via quaternion-similarity spiral, projective wall texture accumulation, SAM3/SAM-3D-Objects-based object instantiation, and depth-edge-recall image validation combined with geometry-regularized 3DGS optimization.

Extensive ablations (Table 2, Fig. 5) convincingly isolate the contribution of each conditioning modality (depth only vs. +objects vs. +walls+bboxes vs. full) and each 3DGS optimization/validation component, showing the full pipeline is needed for both local object consistency and global structural consistency.

Thorough comparison against a wide range of recent, relevant baselines spanning layout-guided (SpatialGen), video-diffusion (WorldExplorer, FlexWorld), iterative lifting (WonderWorld), and panorama-to-3D (DreamScene360, LayerPano3D) approaches, using both automatic metrics and a 31-participant perceptual study with strong, consistent preference for the proposed method (96.2% average).

Additional analyses (backbone-agnosticism across Flux2-klein and Nano Banana Pro, per-scene scaling/cost, navigability via occupancy-grid rasterization, layout-LLM backend ablation) strengthen the practical credibility and robustness claims of the approach.

Clear, well-organized presentation with a thorough appendix (implementation details, prompts, perceptual study protocol, baseline setup) that aids reproducibility of the method design, even if some proprietary components remain a concern.
weaknesses: The pipeline depends on several proprietary, closed-source components (Claude Opus for layout generation, Nano Banana Pro for main appearance synthesis) for its best-performing configuration, which limits exact reproducibility even though the authors show a fully local alternative (Flux2-klein) with somewhat weaker but still competitive results.

The system comprises many hand-engineered heuristic stages (spatial validity sampling rules, object placement collision/overlap resolution, camera pruning by angular redundancy, occlusion/room-based texture filtering) whose individual robustness and sensitivity to hyperparameters are not deeply analyzed beyond the main conditioning-modality ablation.

3D-consistency claims rely heavily on a perceptual study (31 participants) and self-referential geometric metrics (reprojection/alignment against the method's own mesh scaffold); there is no validation against real-world ground-truth 3D scans or independent geometric benchmarks, so absolute geometric accuracy (versus merely internal consistency) is not established.

Comparisons to baselines not designed for multi-room generation are somewhat asymmetric (single-room methods evaluated on a room extracted from a multi-room layout), which the paper acknowledges but which nonetheless makes some quantitative gaps less directly interpretable.

End-to-end runtime/cost for the full multi-room pipeline (LLM layout generation, iterative per-room diffusion sampling, SAM3/SAM-3D-Objects reconstruction, mesh-guided 3DGS optimization) appears substantial, and while Table A3 partially addresses scaling, a clearer total wall-clock/resource comparison against baselines would better contextualize practicality.

Object geometry quality is bounded by SAM-3D-Objects, which the authors note can produce incomplete back faces or coarse textures; this could limit fidelity in some viewpoints and is not deeply quantified beyond qualitative observation.
